title: Design Quarterly 133: “Does It Make Sense?”
lede: April Greiman’s issue of the Walker Art Center’s journal, made on a Macintosh as a single fold-out poster: a life-size bitmap self-portrait among layers of type, symbols, and video images.
summary: A fold-out issue with a pixelated nude self-portrait, spaced typewriter-style lines, symbols, and video stills. April Greiman, Walker Art Center, 1986.

source.label: People’s Graphic Design Archive: Design Quarterly #133

evidence.note: Inspected the People’s Graphic Design Archive photographs of the front and back of one opened copy (1440 × 474 and 1440 × 485) in scratchpad copies. The owner of the copy is not stated. Only the larger type is readable at this size. Not stored.

styles.note: Clear example of the style’s move to the computer: layered fragments, spaced lines of type, and bars, made in MacDraw.
Partial fit: the early Macintosh bitmap self-portrait shows visible square pixels, but the layout is New Wave.

context: Walker Art Center text quoted by the People’s Graphic Design Archive says the usual 32 pages were treated as a two-foot-by-six-foot, double-sided fold-out, and that Greiman used MacDraw to combine video images and type and to tile pages into a pixelated, life-size double self-portrait. [People’s Graphic Design Archive](https://peoplesgdarchive.org/item/1804/does-it-make-sense-design-quarterly-133).
Greiman’s own page names Mildred Friedman as editor and says the type was set on a Macintosh and LaserWriter. [aprilgreiman.com](https://www.aprilgreiman.com/does-it-make-sense).
observed: The front is dark violet on cream. A life-size nude figure made of coarse bitmap dots lies across the whole sheet.
Around the figure float a spiral galaxy, hands, a brain, orbits, planet symbols, small photographs, and a black panel with a moon.
A bitmap block at the top right holds large pixel numerals and “the spiritual double” in a monospaced face.
A line of words runs along the bottom edge on a ruled scale: “proton . neutron . electron . moron . milli . micro …”, with wide gaps and full stops between the words.
“live where you can.” sits upside down on a white bar.
The back has large colour video stills, a yellow ground, a dot-screen cloud in orange, blue text in a slab face, and narrow columns of small text.
interpretation: The issue keeps the style’s layering, bars, and spaced lines, but the type is often monospaced or slab, and bitmap dots replace film screens. It is a partial fit that marks the end of the period and the start of digital postmodern design.
The monospaced lines here are one reason the fingerprint should not treat a small share of monospaced type as a counter-sign by itself.
borrow: Run a spaced-out line of words along a ruled scale at the page edge.
Build one large figure from coarse dots and lay small symbols over it.
Turn one short phrase upside down on a white bar.

rights.statement: No image is stored. April Greiman is living, so the design is in copyright. The photographs’ owner is not stated.
